name: Deer antler velvet spray

lead: Deer antler velvet spray is a supplement made from the soft tissue of growing deer antlers, marketed to athletes and lifters as a source of IGF-1, a growth-related hormone. Users hope for quicker recovery and more training volume, which would feed muscle gain.

It gained wide attention in January 2013 after a Sports Illustrated report linked NFL player Ray Lewis to it; he denied using it. Research is sparse: a small 2003 study over three weeks of strength training found only slight knee strength gains, and experts question how much active IGF-1 survives in a spray.

paras: It is sold as a sublingual spray (also pills or powder) and taken as a recovery or training supplement, often among bodybuilders and athletes alongside conventional training and diet.

A 2014 case report described central serous chorioretinopathy, a retinal condition, in a healthy man that resolved after he stopped the spray. IGF-1 is banned in the NFL and by anti-doping bodies, and clinicians have warned about growth-hormone-type side effects. The spray is sold as a supplement, so the amount of IGF-1 is unclear.

angle.text: Users take it for recovery and training support; any physique benefit is via more training, and the active-ingredient content is uncertain.

lead: Deer antler velvet spray is a sublingual supplement derived from the velvet of growing deer antlers. Sellers market it as a source of IGF-1, a hormone involved in tissue growth, and lifters and athletes use it hoping to recover faster, train more and so build muscle [1][2].

It entered public view in January 2013, when a Sports Illustrated report linked Baltimore Ravens player Ray Lewis to the product after a triceps injury; Lewis and the team denied wrongdoing [1][2]. The seller argued the product helps athletes naturally [2].

Research is limited. A 2003 study of 38 men over three weeks of strength training found slight knee strength and endurance gains with the powder form and no significant overall benefit [2]. A 2014 case report associated the spray with central serous chorioretinopathy [3].
infobox: Sold as supplement; IGF-1 banned in NFL

paras: Users take it for recovery, joint comfort and muscle support. In 2013 coverage, an orthopedic surgeon noted IGF-1 'definitely has the potential to increase healing and recovery' but said he did not know whether the spray contained enough to matter [2].
A 2003 study of 38 men found slight knee strength and endurance gains with powder over three weeks, but no significant overall benefit, and called for more research [2].

A 2014 case report described central serous chorioretinopathy in a healthy man using the spray, resolving after he stopped; the authors suggested agents containing IGF-1 may be correlated with the condition [3].

The Ray Lewis report made the spray a punchline on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation in 2013, where users joked about it and some asked whether it does anything [4]. Because it is sold as a supplement, the FDA does not regulate it like a drug, and the amount of IGF-1 is unclear; IGF-1 is banned by the NFL [2].
Besides the retinal case report [3], a surgeon cautioned that IGF-1 may share growth-hormone side effects such as cardiomyopathy and liver disease with recreational use [2].

lore.intro: On T Nation the spray is mostly a joke tied to 2013 doping stories, with a few members asking sincerely if it works [4].
